title: Interpret an audit report finding
brief:
A district hospital ran a monthly clinical audit on postnatal care documentation. The measure: **proportion of postnatal women with a completed postnatal check recorded within 6 hours of delivery.** The audit covered 40 records over 4 weeks.

| Week | Records audited | Criterion met | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 1 | 10 | 4 | 40% |
| Week 2 | 10 | 6 | 60% |
| Week 3 | 10 | 3 | 30% |
| Week 4 | 10 | 5 | 50% |

**Overall: 18 of 40 = 45%.** The hospital target is 90%.

task.stem: Which interpretation and next action is most appropriate?

options.label: The 45% overall rate is well below the 90% target, but the variation across weeks (30–60%) suggests the problem is inconsistent — not a uniform failure. The priority action is to investigate the process: when and why do checks get missed, and is it the same staff, shift, or day of the week each time?
The audit shows the hospital is improving: 40% in Week 1, 50% in Week 4. Continue monitoring and the target will be reached in time.
The overall rate is 45%, which is too low. The correct response is to set a higher target — 95% — to motivate the team.
Four weeks is too short to draw any conclusion. Repeat the audit for 3 months before taking any action.

debrief.correct: Correct. The 45% rate is a significant gap from 90%, and the week-to-week variation (30%–60%) is the key signal — it tells you the system is inconsistent, not uniformly failing. That inconsistency is a diagnostic clue: something is different on some days or shifts. Investigating *when* and *why* failures cluster is the right first step before designing an intervention. A run chart over more weeks would reveal whether the variation is random or patterned.
debrief.wrong: Option B misreads the data as a trend: Week 1 = 40%, Week 4 = 50% — but Weeks 2 and 3 go up then down. There is no consistent upward trend; that is common-cause variation. Option C confuses motivation with system design — raising a target never fixes a process. Option D delays action unnecessarily; 40 records is enough to identify a serious gap and begin investigation, even if more data will sharpen the picture.
debrief.rule_cited: Audit interpretation — common-cause vs assignable-cause variation. Provost & Murray ch. 3; IHI QI 104.
